newsitem.title: SIERRA LEONE: More than 80 died in Sierra Leone hunters battle.
newsitem.headline: More than 80 died in Sierra Leone hunters battle.

text.p: Eighty bodies have been found after weekend fighting between the Sierra Leone army and a hunters' militia in the eastern town of Kenema, a hospital source said on Tuesday.
A military source said that fresh battles had also erupted in the north where at least six people were killed.

"Hospital staff and the International Red Cross in Kenema have discovered the bodies of 30 civilians, 30 soldiers and 20 Kamajors (hunters) and we are looking for more," the hospital source said by telephone from Kenema, 200 km (125 miles) from the capital Freetown.
The military source reported battles between troops and hunters at Camp Charlie on Sunday and Matotoka on Tuesday.
Matotoka is 140 miles (220 km) from Freetown. "At least six Kamajors and two government soldiers have been killed in bitter fighting," the source said.
Fighting at the army's main military camp in the north, Camp Charlie, killed at least 14 people on Sunday when soldiers fought with a seperate hunters' militia known as Kapras.

There is traditional rivalry between the hunters and regular troops who fought together against rebels of the Revolutionary United Front, but no immediate cause is known for the most recent clashes in the poverty-stricken West African state.

Fighting broke out in Kenema on Saturday, forcing aid agencies to evacuate staff by helicopter as hunters and soldiers traded rocket-propelled grenades and heavy machine gun fire in the streets of the diamond-mining town.
Aid agencies said that although fighting in Kenema stopped on Monday the streets were still tense.
They said more than 70,000 people who were recently resettled in nearby towns and villages after years of civil war had been left without food or medical supplies by their pull-out.
"We have treated 25 wounded people so far, some of them in very bad shape from gunshot wounds and in need of emergency surgery," said one official of the International Committee of the Red Cross.
To establish the cause of the fighting between the former allies, President Ahmed Tejan Kabbah on Sunday said he had set up a six-man commission of inquiry.

Army chief of staff Lieutenant-Colonel Max Kanga told Reuters that troops were being attacked because the government had not put adequate structures in place to keep the militias under control and punish them if they broke the law.

A peace deal between Tejan Kabbah and rebel leader Foday Sankoh was signed in November to try to end the civil war which erupted in 1991. Implementation of the deal has dragged, threatening to unravel the peace process.
